evaluated.name: SerialRepurchaser_Cheapness_Persistence
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at), 0), 5))
evaluated.hypothesis: Repeated, multi-year net repurchase is a credible (costly, hard-to-fake) signal of managerial conviction, so cheapness accompanied by a long history of net share retirement identifies persistent undervaluation, whereas cheap firms that have never retired shares are more likely value traps.
evaluated.reasoning: A single-year buyback can be opportunistic or cash-driven noise, so the count of net-repurchase years over five years measures the persistence of the financing state and scales the value signal by managerial credibility. Firms that are expensive get a near-zero valuation rank so their repurchase history contributes little, concentrating the signal in the cheap-and-committed corner.

evaluated.name: Value_Payout_ANDgate
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(ADD(dvc, SUB(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), COALESCE(sstk, 0))), MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Mispricing requires joint confirmation: only firms that are simultaneously cheap on a revenue-based price multiple AND are net distributors of cash are reliably undervalued, and only firms that are simultaneously expensive AND net absorbers of equity are reliably overvalued; extremity on one theme alone should not place a firm in the tails.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the rank-sum with a rank product makes the construction a bilinear AND-gate — a firm cheap on sales-to-price but issuing equity is multiplied down toward the middle, which is exactly what the additive version failed to do. Sales-to-price is used instead of book-to-market so the valuation leg is not mechanically tied to the same accumulated-equity accounting that issuance itself inflates, and COALESCE keeps zero-flow firms in the sample.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: FinancingInformativeness_ScaledByCheapness
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), COALESCE(sstk, 0)), at), 1))
evaluated.hypothesis: The information content of an equity-financing decision depends on the price at which it is transacted: retiring shares when the market values the firm far below book is a costly, high-conviction signal, while raising equity at a depressed valuation reveals binding financial constraints and value destruction; among richly valued firms financing flows are growth-driven and carry little mispricing content.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a pure interaction term with no additive main effects — the financing variable's slope is scaled by the cheapness rank, so the signal is identically near zero for expensive firms and cannot be reproduced by summing E/P and net-payout yield. It changes the economics from "buybacks are good" to "the same financing action means opposite things at different prices," and winsorizing the scaled flow prevents a few extreme repurchase-to-assets observations from driving the spread.

evaluated.name: Conjunction_Corner_CashflowYield_Repurchase
evaluated.expression: SUB(MIN(RANK(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), COALESCE(sstk, 0)), MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), MIN(RANK(NEG(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), COALESCE(sstk, 0)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Only the two diagonal corners are informative — high operating-cash-flow yield together with net share retirement (management buying a cash-generating business the market is discounting) and low cash-flow yield together with net equity issuance (management selling paper the market is overpricing) — while cheap issuers and expensive repurchasers should score near zero because valuation and action disagree.
evaluated.reasoning: The MIN operator makes the score the weaker of the two confirmations, so a firm extreme on one leg alone gets no score, and subtracting the mirror-image conjunction makes the mapping antisymmetric; this now literally implements the "off-diagonal cells carry no signal" hypothesis that the previous indicator version misstated. Using realized operating cash-flow yield rather than book-to-market, and dollar repurchase flows rather than announcement events, separates the test from the announcement-drift-in-value-stocks literature, and the redundant /at scaling inside the conditioning is removed.

evaluated.name: EnterpriseCheapness_ConditionalCapitalFlow

evaluated.reasoning: The indicator gating means the enterprise multiple contributes only where financing agrees, so the test cannot be replicated by an additive average of the enterprise-multiple and external-financing anomalies, and off-diagonal firms receive attenuated (mid-range) rather than extreme scores. Debt financing is measured from the balance-sheet change in dltt+dlc instead of the sparsely populated dltis/dltr flow items, which preserves coverage while keeping the total-capital-flow economics intact.

evaluated.name: ContrarianBuyback_vs_TimedIssuance
evaluated.expression: SUB(MUL(RANK(NEG(GROWTH(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq), 1))), INDICATOR(SUB(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), COALESCE(sstk, 0)), 0)), MUL(RANK(GROWTH(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq), 1)), INDICATOR(SUB(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), 0)))
evaluated.hypothesis: What reveals private information is not the level of the multiple but the direction management trades against its recent move: buying back stock after the price-to-book multiple has collapsed is a contrarian bet that the de-rating is unwarranted, while issuing equity after the multiple has re-rated upward is opportunistic exploitation of a rich price.
evaluated.reasoning: Because the conditioning variable is the one-year *change* in the multiple rather than its level, the resulting spread is a price-path/reversal-flavored bet that FF5 (which contains no momentum or reversal factor) cannot mechanically absorb, addressing the HML-clone problem that killed the gen-0 alphas. The two indicator-gated terms keep the mapping sign-aligned (contrarian repurchasers long, run-up issuers short) with off-diagonal firms receiving attenuated mid-range scores.

evaluated.name: OwnHistoryCheapness_FinancingCorner

evaluated.hypothesis: Managers know their own firm's normal valuation, not the cross-sectional value distribution; repurchasing when book-to-market sits at the top of its own five-year range is a conviction signal even for a firm that is expensive relative to peers, and issuing when the multiple sits at its own five-year peak is a timing signal even for a firm that looks statistically cheap.

evaluated.reasoning: Financing *instability* is a second-moment concept that no FF5 factor proxies for, and interacting it with expensiveness targets the overvaluation half of the story where market-timing incentives bind hardest. evaluated.name: IndustryCheap_NetCapitalReturn_Gate

evaluated.hypothesis: Undervaluation is confirmed only when a cheaply priced firm is a net returner of capital to all claimholders — distributing dividends while shrinking its liability base — whereas a richly priced firm that funds itself by expanding liabilities is being propped up by external capital; the two conditions must hold jointly to signal mispricing.
evaluated.reasoning: Both legs now use one construct per theme — an industry-relative EBITDA-to-price rank and a single net-capital-returned measure (total dividends less the change in the liability ratio) — so there is no long/short asymmetry mixing dividend yield against price-to-book. The multiplicative AND-gate is non-additive (unlike mirrored MIN or complementary-indicator forms, which collapse algebraically to a rank sum), and industry-relative valuation plus liability-flow financing keeps HML/CMA loading low while lt, dvt and at give far broader coverage than cash-flow-statement issuance items.

evaluated.expression: SUB(TS_SUM(MUL(INDICATOR(SUB(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), COALESCE(sstk, 0)), 0), INDICATOR(GROWTH(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1), 0)), 5), TS_SUM(MUL(INDICATOR(SUB(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), 0), INDICATOR(NEG(GROWTH(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)), 0)), 5))
evaluated.hypothesis: What is informative is how often management has repeatedly acted against its own valuation drift: years in which the firm retired shares while its book-to-market was rising (buying into a de-rating) accumulate evidence of genuine undervaluation, while years in which it issued equity while its book-to-market was falling (selling into a re-rating) accumulate evidence of deliberate overvaluation timing.

Because the valuation condition is a within-firm change in the multiple rather than a cross-sectional level, the resulting spread carries little HML exposure, and the four state cells are non-complementary so mixed-history firms land near zero rather than in the tails.

evaluated.hypothesis: Equity issuance means opposite things at opposite prices: a firm selling stock at a multiple far above its industry peers is monetizing overvaluation, whereas a firm forced to sell stock at a below-peer multiple is raising survival capital and its low price already reflects that; the issuance signal should therefore be graded by relative valuation.
evaluated.reasoning: This reverses the conditioning direction of Signals 1–3 — valuation now varies inside the issuer subsample instead of financing varying inside a valuation bucket — so together they identify which variable should condition on which, a design question the archive has never resolved. Industry z-scoring the multiple and assigning non-issuers exactly zero puts them in the middle of the sort, so the tails are cheap issuers versus expensive issuers rather than issuers versus non-issuers, keeping the spread distinct from the published net-issuance anomaly.

evaluated.hypothesis: Holding the need for outside capital fixed, the *source* management chooses reveals its private valuation: a richly priced firm that funds itself with debt rather than equity is telling us it considers its own shares too cheap to sell, whereas one that funds itself with equity at the same high multiple is monetizing an inflated price.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the net-issuance level entirely — both tails contain firms raising external capital at high multiples, so the amount of financing and the investment/asset-growth channel are held roughly constant while only the debt-versus-equity mix varies, which is not the published issuance anomaly. Using the balance-sheet change in dltt+dlc rather than sparse dltis keeps coverage intact, and winsorizing limits the influence of small option-exercise proceeds inside sstk.

evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), MUL(NEG(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1), 1)), INDICATOR(SUB(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), COALESCE(sstk, 0)), 0)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Not all buybacks are informative — only self-funded ones are: a cheap firm retiring shares while simultaneously shrinking its liability base is spending genuine surplus cash on an undervalued asset, whereas a firm borrowing to repurchase is engineering per-share optics and leaves the balance sheet more fragile.

evaluated.name: EarningsYield_x_PersistenceCount_FullPanel
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), 0.02), 5))
evaluated.hypothesis: Bottom-line earnings yield is a valid cheapness anchor for the participation mechanism, and combining it with habitual-transaction conditioning should deliver the mechanism at full panel coverage.

evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashYield_x_ChronicParticipantGate
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), INDICATOR(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), 0.02), 5), 4))
evaluated.hypothesis: If the mechanism is conditioning rather than weighting, its strongest form is a strict gate: cheapness should predict returns among firms that transacted materially in their own shares in every one of the last five years, and carry no information for anyone else.
evaluated.reasoning: This pushes the interpretation that the count amplifier established to its logical endpoint — a pure 0/1 membership test with no magnitude and no gradations, so an alpha comparable to the count version would be the cleanest possible evidence that the interaction is a conditioning effect rather than a rescaled value score. It also yields the most stable portfolio composition of any design in the archive, since membership in the chronic-participant set changes slowly.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: CashYield_x_SerialIssuerPersistence
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(COALESCE(sstk, 0), at), 0.02), 5))
evaluated.hypothesis: Habitual issuance is the stronger half of the participation state: firms that sell stock materially in most years are under continuous market discipline, and among them the cheap ones — those selling equity despite strong cash generation relative to price — are systematically underpriced.

A positive result also matters for interpretation, since it is the opposite of what a naive reading of the net-issuance anomaly predicts and cannot be a repackaged buyback-yield effect.

evaluated.name: EnterpriseCashYield_x_PersistenceCount
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oancf, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), 1), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), 0.02), 5))

evaluated.reasoning: This keeps the cash-flow anchor that has proven far stronger than sales, EBITDA-to-price or earnings-to-price, while removing the one mechanical contamination that remains in the leading signal — a buyback lowers market cap and mechanically raises the equity-based cash yield, which could inflate the interaction. If the alpha survives at similar magnitude, the archive's headline result is a genuine valuation-participation interaction rather than an accounting artifact of the transaction itself.

evaluated.name: CashYield_x_ActiveShareholderDecisionPersistence
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(ADD(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), ABS(DELTA(RATIO(dvt, at), 1))), 0.02), 5))

It also states the mechanism more precisely than the archive's winner — decisions, not transactions per se — and remains a bounded 0–5 conditioner rather than a magnitude weighting, which is the construction the evidence says works best.

considered.name: SerialRepurchaser_Cheapness_Persistence
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(SUB(prstkc, sstk), at), 0), 5))
considered.hypothesis: Repeated, multi-year net repurchase is a credible (costly, hard-to-fake) signal of managerial conviction, so cheapness accompanied by a long history of net share retirement identifies persistent undervaluation, whereas cheap firms that have never retired shares are more likely value traps.
considered.reasoning: A single-year buyback can be opportunistic or cash-driven noise, so the count of net-repurchase years over five years measures the persistence of the financing state and scales the value signal by managerial credibility. Firms that are expensive get a near-zero valuation rank so their repurchase history contributes little, concentrating the signal in the cheap-and-committed corner.

considered.name: Value_Payout_ANDgate
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(sale, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(ADD(dvc, SUB(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), COALESCE(sstk, 0))), MUL(prcc_f, csho))))
considered.hypothesis: Mispricing requires joint confirmation: only firms that are simultaneously cheap on a revenue-based price multiple AND are net distributors of cash are reliably undervalued, and only firms that are simultaneously expensive AND net absorbers of equity are reliably overvalued; extremity on one theme alone should not place a firm in the tails.
considered.reasoning: Replacing the rank-sum with a rank product makes the construction a bilinear AND-gate — a firm cheap on sales-to-price but issuing equity is multiplied down toward the middle, which is exactly what the additive version failed to do. Sales-to-price is used instead of book-to-market so the valuation leg is not mechanically tied to the same accumulated-equity accounting that issuance itself inflates, and COALESCE keeps zero-flow firms in the sample.

considered.name: FinancingInformativeness_ScaledByCheapness
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), COALESCE(sstk, 0)), at), 1))
considered.hypothesis: The information content of an equity-financing decision depends on the price at which it is transacted: retiring shares when the market values the firm far below book is a costly, high-conviction signal, while raising equity at a depressed valuation reveals binding financial constraints and value destruction; among richly valued firms financing flows are growth-driven and carry little mispricing content.
considered.reasoning: This is a pure interaction term with no additive main effects — the financing variable's slope is scaled by the cheapness rank, so the signal is identically near zero for expensive firms and cannot be reproduced by summing E/P and net-payout yield. It changes the economics from "buybacks are good" to "the same financing action means opposite things at different prices," and winsorizing the scaled flow prevents a few extreme repurchase-to-assets observations from driving the spread.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Conjunction_Corner_CashflowYield_Repurchase
considered.expression: SUB(MIN(RANK(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), COALESCE(sstk, 0)), MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), MIN(RANK(NEG(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), COALESCE(sstk, 0)), MUL(prcc_f, csho))))))
considered.hypothesis: Only the two diagonal corners are informative — high operating-cash-flow yield together with net share retirement (management buying a cash-generating business the market is discounting) and low cash-flow yield together with net equity issuance (management selling paper the market is overpricing) — while cheap issuers and expensive repurchasers should score near zero because valuation and action disagree.
considered.reasoning: The MIN operator makes the score the weaker of the two confirmations, so a firm extreme on one leg alone gets no score, and subtracting the mirror-image conjunction makes the mapping antisymmetric; this now literally implements the "off-diagonal cells carry no signal" hypothesis that the previous indicator version misstated. Using realized operating cash-flow yield rather than book-to-market, and dollar repurchase flows rather than announcement events, separates the test from the announcement-drift-in-value-stocks literature, and the redundant /at scaling inside the conditioning is removed.

considered.name: EnterpriseCheapness_ConditionalCapitalFlow
considered.expression: SUB(MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), INDICATOR(NEG(RATIO(ADD(SUB(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1)), at)), 0)), MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che)))), INDICATOR(RATIO(ADD(SUB(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1)), at), 0)))

considered.reasoning: The indicator gating means the enterprise multiple contributes only where financing agrees, so the test cannot be replicated by an additive average of the enterprise-multiple and external-financing anomalies, and off-diagonal firms receive attenuated (mid-range) rather than extreme scores. Debt financing is measured from the balance-sheet change in dltt+dlc instead of the sparsely populated dltis/dltr flow items, which preserves coverage while keeping the total-capital-flow economics intact.

considered.name: OneSided_ShareCount_Valuation_Corners
considered.expression: SUB(MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), MUL(NEG(MA(GROWTH(csho, 1), 3)), INDICATOR(NEG(MA(GROWTH(csho, 1), 3)), 0))), MUL(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), MUL(MA(GROWTH(csho, 1), 3), INDICATOR(MA(GROWTH(csho, 1), 3), 0))))

considered.reasoning: The previous version's long leg was populated by glamour repurchasers because a signed issuance average was multiplied by a price-to-book rank; here the dilution and shrinkage channels are separated with one-sided indicator gating so the long extreme is cheap share-shrinkers and the short extreme is expensive diluters, matching the stated story. Using the three-year average of share-count growth measures financing persistence with near-universal coverage (prcc_f, csho, ceq only) rather than relying on cash-flow-statement issuance items.

considered.name: ContrarianBuyback_vs_TimedIssuance
considered.expression: SUB(MUL(RANK(NEG(GROWTH(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq), 1))), INDICATOR(SUB(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), COALESCE(sstk, 0)), 0)), MUL(RANK(GROWTH(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq), 1)), INDICATOR(SUB(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), 0)))
considered.hypothesis: What reveals private information is not the level of the multiple but the direction management trades against its recent move: buying back stock after the price-to-book multiple has collapsed is a contrarian bet that the de-rating is unwarranted, while issuing equity after the multiple has re-rated upward is opportunistic exploitation of a rich price.
considered.reasoning: Because the conditioning variable is the one-year *change* in the multiple rather than its level, the resulting spread is a price-path/reversal-flavored bet that FF5 (which contains no momentum or reversal factor) cannot mechanically absorb, addressing the HML-clone problem that killed the gen-0 alphas. The two indicator-gated terms keep the mapping sign-aligned (contrarian repurchasers long, run-up issuers short) with off-diagonal firms receiving attenuated mid-range scores.

considered.name: OwnHistoryCheapness_FinancingCorner
considered.expression: SUB(MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5), INDICATOR(SUB(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), COALESCE(sstk, 0)), 0)), MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq), 5), INDICATOR(SUB(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), 0)))
considered.hypothesis: Managers know their own firm's normal valuation, not the cross-sectional value distribution; repurchasing when book-to-market sits at the top of its own five-year range is a conviction signal even for a firm that is expensive relative to peers, and issuing when the multiple sits at its own five-year peak is a timing signal even for a firm that looks statistically cheap.
considered.reasoning: Replacing the cross-sectional valuation rank with a within-firm time-series rank removes the permanent value tilt (every firm's TS_RANK cycles through 0–1), so the long-short portfolio should carry near-zero HML loading and any spread must show up as FF5 alpha rather than being absorbed. This deliberately isolates one design choice relative to the gen-0 EnterpriseCheapness structure (which had the strongest FMB t but zero alpha): cross-sectional versus own-history valuation conditioning.

considered.name: BuybackImpulse_in_CheapFirms
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), COALESCE(sstk, 0)), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1), 1))
considered.hypothesis: The level of net repurchase yield is highly persistent and already capitalized, so the informative event is the year-over-year *escalation* of net share retirement; an escalation by a cheap firm is fresh evidence of undervaluation, while a cheap firm abruptly switching from buybacks to issuance signals deteriorating fundamentals or forced financing.
considered.reasoning: This is a pure interaction term with no additive main effects, and because the financing input is a first difference centered near zero the portfolio spread is a financing-news bet inside the value segment rather than a payout-level bet that CMA/RMW would explain. It directly diagnoses why the gen-0 level-based version of this same structure had a flat FMB slope (t=0.40): if the level is stale, the change should carry the signal.

considered.name: Glamour_FinancingInstability
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), VOL(RATIO(SUB(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), 5))
considered.hypothesis: Opportunistic market timing shows up as erratic, lumpy equity financing rather than a steady policy; high-multiple firms whose net equity issuance is volatile are repeatedly tapping the market when windows open, which marks them as overvalued, whereas high-multiple firms with stable financing policies are genuine growth compounders.
considered.reasoning: Financing *instability* is a second-moment concept that no FF5 factor proxies for, and interacting it with expensiveness targets the overvaluation half of the story where market-timing incentives bind hardest. The construction is deliberately asymmetric — the short extreme is glamour firms with erratic issuance and the long side is populated by cheap and/or financing-stable firms — which tests whether the alpha in this theme lives on the short leg, information the gen-0 batch could not provide.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: IndustryCheap_NetCapitalReturn_Gate
considered.expression: MUL(IND_RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(SUB(RATIO(dvt, at), DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Undervaluation is confirmed only when a cheaply priced firm is a net returner of capital to all claimholders — distributing dividends while shrinking its liability base — whereas a richly priced firm that funds itself by expanding liabilities is being propped up by external capital; the two conditions must hold jointly to signal mispricing.
considered.reasoning: Both legs now use one construct per theme — an industry-relative EBITDA-to-price rank and a single net-capital-returned measure (total dividends less the change in the liability ratio) — so there is no long/short asymmetry mixing dividend yield against price-to-book. The multiplicative AND-gate is non-additive (unlike mirrored MIN or complementary-indicator forms, which collapse algebraically to a rank sum), and industry-relative valuation plus liability-flow financing keeps HML/CMA loading low while lt, dvt and at give far broader coverage than cash-flow-statement issuance items.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: JointStatePersistence_BuyIntoWeakness
considered.expression: SUB(TS_SUM(MUL(INDICATOR(SUB(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), COALESCE(sstk, 0)), 0), INDICATOR(GROWTH(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1), 0)), 5), TS_SUM(MUL(INDICATOR(SUB(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), 0), INDICATOR(NEG(GROWTH(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)), 0)), 5))
considered.hypothesis: What is informative is how often management has repeatedly acted against its own valuation drift: years in which the firm retired shares while its book-to-market was rising (buying into a de-rating) accumulate evidence of genuine undervaluation, while years in which it issued equity while its book-to-market was falling (selling into a re-rating) accumulate evidence of deliberate overvaluation timing.
considered.reasoning: The interaction is formed inside the temporal sum as a product of two indicators, so the score counts occupancy of the joint valuation-financing state and cannot be decomposed into a valuation main effect plus a financing main effect — the algebraic collapse the critic identified in the mirrored-count version. Because the valuation condition is a within-firm change in the multiple rather than a cross-sectional level, the resulting spread carries little HML exposure, and the four state cells are non-complementary so mixed-history firms land near zero rather than in the tails.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: WithinCheap_LiabilityFlowSpread
considered.expression: MUL(NEG(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1), 1)), INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.5))
considered.hypothesis: Within the cheap half of the market, the distinguishing feature of a genuine bargain is that it is shrinking its claim base rather than absorbing new external capital; cheap firms expanding liabilities are cheap because they are being recapitalized, not because the market is wrong.
considered.reasoning: This keeps the value-neutral conditioning design of Signal 1 but switches the financing channel from cash-flow-statement equity flows to the balance-sheet liability ratio, which is reported by essentially all firms — testing whether the thin 0.13 coverage of prstkc/sstk designs, not the economics, was limiting portfolio stability. Using an EBITDA-to-price gate rather than book-to-market also checks that the conditioning result is not an artifact of one valuation proxy.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: WithinIssuer_ValuationSpread
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), 1), INDICATOR(SUB(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), 0))
considered.hypothesis: Equity issuance means opposite things at opposite prices: a firm selling stock at a multiple far above its industry peers is monetizing overvaluation, whereas a firm forced to sell stock at a below-peer multiple is raising survival capital and its low price already reflects that; the issuance signal should therefore be graded by relative valuation.
considered.reasoning: This reverses the conditioning direction of Signals 1–3 — valuation now varies inside the issuer subsample instead of financing varying inside a valuation bucket — so together they identify which variable should condition on which, a design question the archive has never resolved. Industry z-scoring the multiple and assigning non-issuers exactly zero puts them in the middle of the sort, so the tails are cheap issuers versus expensive issuers rather than issuers versus non-issuers, keeping the spread distinct from the published net-issuance anomaly.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: GlamourFunding_DebtOverEquity_Timing
considered.expression: MUL(NEG(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(COALESCE(sstk, 0), at), DELTA(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), at), 1)), 1)), INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), 0.5))
considered.hypothesis: Holding the need for outside capital fixed, the *source* management chooses reveals its private valuation: a richly priced firm that funds itself with debt rather than equity is telling us it considers its own shares too cheap to sell, whereas one that funds itself with equity at the same high multiple is monetizing an inflated price.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the net-issuance level entirely — both tails contain firms raising external capital at high multiples, so the amount of financing and the investment/asset-growth channel are held roughly constant while only the debt-versus-equity mix varies, which is not the published issuance anomaly. Using the balance-sheet change in dltt+dlc rather than sparse dltis keeps coverage intact, and winsorizing limits the influence of small option-exercise proceeds inside sstk.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: BuybackFundingQuality_GradedByCheapness
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), MUL(NEG(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(lt, at), 1), 1)), INDICATOR(SUB(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), COALESCE(sstk, 0)), 0)))
considered.hypothesis: Not all buybacks are informative — only self-funded ones are: a cheap firm retiring shares while simultaneously shrinking its liability base is spending genuine surplus cash on an undervalued asset, whereas a firm borrowing to repurchase is engineering per-share optics and leaves the balance sheet more fragile.
considered.reasoning: Every firm in both tails is a net repurchaser, so the buyback/net-issuance anomaly is held fixed by construction and the spread is driven by the funding source, with cheapness grading the magnitude — this is a different question from the accepted within-cheap liability-flow signal, which does not condition on repurchase activity at all. Non-repurchasers receive exactly zero and sit in the uninformative middle, so the tails are economically homogeneous portfolios rather than a tied mass.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DividendSignal_WithinCheapEarningsYield
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(dvt, at), 1), 1), INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 0.5))
considered.hypothesis: For firms already priced cheaply on earnings, a rising dividend is a costly commitment that the depressed earnings are sustainable, while a dividend cut is management conceding the earnings base is impaired — so the change in distributions separates undervalued cheap firms from value traps.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the size-subsample variant with a genuinely different financing channel — dividend-signaling rather than share issuance — and both tails lie in the high-earnings-yield half, keeping the spread value-neutral instead of an HML clone. Because dvt is reported far more broadly than prstkc/sstk and the signal is a first difference around zero, coverage rises rather than halves and the sort is not a payout-level (published dividend-yield) bet.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ExternallyFundedPayout_at_HighMultiple
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), WINSOR(SUB(ADD(RATIO(dvt, at), RATIO(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), at)), RATIO(oancf, at)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Distributions that exceed internally generated cash must be funded by outside capital; a highly valued firm sustaining dividends and buybacks it cannot cover from operations is maintaining the appearance of shareholder returns with investors' own money, which marks overvaluation.
considered.reasoning: Replacing MIN of two non-negative flows with the signed gap between total distributions and operating cash flow removes the tied mass at zero and gives a continuous, economically interpretable measure of payout that must be externally financed, so both tails are real portfolios. Because the excess-payout term is scaled by assets and the conditioning term is the price-to-book rank, the signal targets the overvaluation half of the story with a funding-sustainability mechanism no single-theme payout or issuance variable captures.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: GlamourGated_PayoutCoverageShortfall
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(SUB(ADD(RATIO(dvt, at), RATIO(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), at)), RATIO(oancf, at)), 1), INDICATOR(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), 0.5))
considered.hypothesis: The payout-sustainability signal is informative only where the price embeds optimistic expectations: within the expensive half of the market, firms distributing beyond internal cash generation underperform firms retaining a large internal surplus, while among cheap firms the same gap mostly reflects cyclical earnings.
considered.reasoning: Replacing the continuous price-to-book weight with a hard median gate forces both tails strictly inside the glamour half, making the spread fully value-neutral instead of only approximately so, and cleanly separating "interaction" from "valuation-weighted main effect". Cheap firms are parked at exactly zero in the middle of the sort, so if this version retains the winner's alpha the interaction claim is validated, and if it loses it, the archived result was partly a valuation main effect.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: EnterpriseRichness_PayoutShortfall
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che), sale)), WINSOR(SUB(ADD(RATIO(dvt, at), RATIO(COALESCE(prstkc, 0), at)), RATIO(oancf, at)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Firms that fund distributions externally simultaneously become more levered, so an equity-only multiple mismeasures how richly the *whole business* is priced; grading the payout shortfall by enterprise-value-to-sales identifies overvalued businesses whose apparent shareholder returns are debt-financed.
considered.reasoning: This isolates the valuation-metric axis of the winning mechanism: because uncovered payout mechanically raises leverage, price-to-book and the shortfall are entangled, whereas EV/sales prices the enterprise and is not inflated by the buyback itself. Using sales in the denominator also avoids the negative-book-equity distortion the critic flagged elsewhere, so the conditioning variable is well-defined for exactly the distressed-glamour firms that matter most.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: NormalCashFlow_PayoutShortfall_Glamour
considered.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ceq)), WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(ADD(dvt, COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Sustainability should be judged against normal, not current, cash generation: a highly valued firm distributing more than its three-year average operating cash flow is structurally over-distributing, whereas one exceeding a single depressed year may simply be smoothing through a cyclical trough.
considered.reasoning: The temporal smoothing is required by the mechanism rather than decorative — the economic claim is about chronic dependence on outside funding, which a one-year cash-flow comparison conflates with transitory dips — so this variant should raise the signal-to-noise of the same interaction and improve FMB precision. It also predicts a lower turnover, more stable long-short composition than the one-year version, which speaks to the objective's stability diagnostic.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: MaterialIssuers_RelativeSalesMultiple

considered.reasoning: The archive has tested sales-to-price (flat, fmb 0.08) and EBITDA-to-price (flat, fmb 0.06) at full coverage but never earnings-to-price, so this is a genuinely new anchor and the cleanest remaining test of whether the winning result is about *cash* valuation or about the post-1988 sample. A strong outcome would give a full-coverage version of the mechanism; a flat one would establish that only cash-based or enterprise-based anchors transmit.

considered.name: CashYield_x_TransactionPersistenceCount
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), 0.02), 5))
considered.hypothesis: Habitual participation is a firm attribute: firms that have transacted materially in their own shares in most of the last five years operate under continuous scrutiny of their own valuation, so cheapness is more informative for them than for occasional participants.
considered.reasoning: The earlier persistence-count attempt failed, but it was paired with the sales anchor that we now know is inert (fmb 0.08), so the state-versus-event question has never been tested with a working anchor — and the engagement-surprise result argues for the event view, making this the decisive counter-test. A bounded 0–5 count amplifier also produces the most stable portfolio composition of any amplifier tried, which matters for the reliability of the alpha t-statistic.

considered.name: CashYield_x_DividendIntensity_Discriminant
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), WINSOR(RATIO(dvt, at), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Dividends move cash to shareholders but involve no transaction in the firm's own shares at a market price, so if the amplification mechanism is really about a valuation gap being monetised, dividend intensity should amplify cheapness far less than share turnover does; if instead any non-negative payout-like weight works equally well, the whole family is a reweighted value signal.
considered.reasoning: This directly confronts the critic's alternative explanation — that every non-negative amplifier produces the same statistics because it is merely magnitude-weighting a cash-flow-yield value signal — by substituting a financing flow of comparable size and dispersion that carries no own-share-transaction content. It is the cheapest decisive test available with one generation remaining, since a materially weaker result establishes the specificity of the participation channel while a comparable result would tell us to stop treating the amplifier as economically meaningful.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: EnterpriseYield_x_ActivityIndicator_FullPanel
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), 1), INDICATOR(IND_RANK(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at)), 0.7))
considered.hypothesis: Cheapness at the enterprise level predicts returns only among firms that are heavy transactors of their own shares by their industry's standards; firms below that threshold carry no valuation signal at all, so the interaction is a conditioning effect rather than a magnitude weighting.
considered.reasoning: Replacing the continuous amplifier with a 0/1 industry-relative activity gate removes magnitude weighting entirely, so a surviving alpha cannot be dismissed as a rescaled value signal — and it runs at full 0.14 coverage on the only anchor that works outside the post-1988 oancf subsample, attacking the archive's binding coverage constraint rather than shuffling amplifier variants whose statistics the archive shows to be indistinguishable. Inactive firms are parked at exactly zero, so both tails consist solely of heavy transactors.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashYield_x_BookEquityBaseTurnover
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), ceq), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Participation should be measured against the equity base being transacted rather than against total assets, since an identical share issue means far more for a firm with a thin equity base than for a heavily capitalised one, and asset-scaling conflates the transaction with leverage and asset intensity.
considered.reasoning: This keeps the economic argument of the flagged version — the equity base is the right denominator for own-share activity — while deflating by book equity rather than market capitalisation, so the product no longer loads mechanically on the inverse squared price and cannot be confounded with a low-price microcap tilt. Comparison against the assets-scaled parent then isolates the deflator question cleanly, with no price appearing twice in the expression.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashYield_x_DebtIssuanceOnly
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), WINSOR(RATIO(COALESCE(dltis, 0), at), 1))
considered.hypothesis: If the amplifier works because informed outside capital providers are actively pricing the firm, then gross long-term debt raised should amplify cheapness on its own; if it works because management is trading its own mispriced equity, debt issuance should not.
considered.reasoning: A debt-only amplifier is the internally consistent version of the test I mis-specified by summing equity and debt flows, since it shares no equity-transaction information with the archive's winners and dltis is an actual gross capital-raising flow rather than the balance-sheet churn proxy that gave a strong slope but weak alpha. Paired with the dividend discriminant in Signal 1, the two together identify whether the channel is lender scrutiny, shareholder-transaction scrutiny, or neither.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: EnterpriseYield_x_PersistenceCount_FullPanel
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), 1), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), 0.02), 5))
considered.hypothesis: Enterprise-level cheapness predicts returns among habitual participants in their own equity market, so the conditioning mechanism should hold across the full panel and not only in the post-1988 window where operating cash flow is reported.
considered.reasoning: The count amplifier is the archive's strongest and most economically interpretable conditioner (fmb 4.30, alpha +4.9%) but has only ever been run on the coverage-limited oancf anchor, while the enterprise anchor is the only full-panel anchor with a reliable slope — this pairing is untested and directly attacks the one remaining weakness of the leading result. Enterprise value is also not deflated by the share transactions used to build the amplifier, so anchor and conditioner stay economically separate.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: EarningsYield_x_PersistenceCount_FullPanel
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(ib, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), 0.02), 5))
considered.hypothesis: Bottom-line earnings yield is a valid cheapness anchor for the participation mechanism, and combining it with habitual-transaction conditioning should deliver the mechanism at full panel coverage.
considered.reasoning: Earnings-to-price with the weaker magnitude amplifier already produced +3.8% alpha at t=3.01 and 0.143 coverage — the best full-panel alpha in the archive — despite a flat FMB slope, so upgrading its amplifier to the count conditioner that lifted the cash anchor from +4.2% to +4.9% is the highest-expected-value full-coverage test available. Comparing it with Signal 1 also settles whether the full-panel anchor should be equity earnings or enterprise profitability.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashYield_x_ChronicParticipantGate
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), INDICATOR(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), 0.02), 5), 4))
considered.hypothesis: If the mechanism is conditioning rather than weighting, its strongest form is a strict gate: cheapness should predict returns among firms that transacted materially in their own shares in every one of the last five years, and carry no information for anyone else.
considered.reasoning: This pushes the interpretation that the count amplifier established to its logical endpoint — a pure 0/1 membership test with no magnitude and no gradations, so an alpha comparable to the count version would be the cleanest possible evidence that the interaction is a conditioning effect rather than a rescaled value score. It also yields the most stable portfolio composition of any design in the archive, since membership in the chronic-participant set changes slowly.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashYield_x_SerialIssuerPersistence
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(COALESCE(sstk, 0), at), 0.02), 5))
considered.hypothesis: Habitual issuance is the stronger half of the participation state: firms that sell stock materially in most years are under continuous market discipline, and among them the cheap ones — those selling equity despite strong cash generation relative to price — are systematically underpriced.
considered.reasoning: The single-year decomposition showed the issuance leg carried the larger alpha (+4.4% versus +3.1% for repurchases), so decomposing the count amplifier by direction tests whether that asymmetry persists in the state variable that now defines the best signal. A positive result also matters for interpretation, since it is the opposite of what a naive reading of the net-issuance anomaly predicts and cannot be a repackaged buyback-yield effect.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: EnterpriseCashYield_x_PersistenceCount
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oancf, SUB(ADD(MUL(prcc_f, csho), ADD(dltt, dlc)), che))), 1), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), 0.02), 5))
considered.hypothesis: Operating cash flow accrues to all capital providers, so pricing it against enterprise value rather than market capitalisation is the internally consistent cheapness measure, and it is immune to the mechanical shrinkage of the equity base caused by the very repurchases that define the amplifier.
considered.reasoning: This keeps the cash-flow anchor that has proven far stronger than sales, EBITDA-to-price or earnings-to-price, while removing the one mechanical contamination that remains in the leading signal — a buyback lowers market cap and mechanically raises the equity-based cash yield, which could inflate the interaction. If the alpha survives at similar magnitude, the archive's headline result is a genuine valuation-participation interaction rather than an accounting artifact of the transaction itself.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: CashYield_x_ActiveShareholderDecisionPersistence
considered.expression: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), 1), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(ADD(RATIO(ADD(COALESCE(sstk, 0), COALESCE(prstkc, 0)), at), ABS(DELTA(RATIO(dvt, at), 1))), 0.02), 5))
considered.hypothesis: What conditions the valuation signal is the frequency of active decisions taken toward shareholders — materially transacting in the firm's own shares or materially resetting the payout rate — rather than the static characteristic of being a dividend payer; cheapness is informative for firms whose equity policy is repeatedly re-decided and priced.
considered.reasoning: Replacing the dividend *level* with the absolute year-over-year *change* in the payout rate removes the defect the critic identified: a steady payer no longer trips the counter every year, since only a policy shift exceeding two percent of assets qualifies, so the count cannot degenerate into a dividend-payer indicator with its size, profitability and low-volatility loadings. It also states the mechanism more precisely than the archive's winner — decisions, not transactions per se — and remains a bounded 0–5 conditioner rather than a magnitude weighting, which is the construction the evidence says works best.
considered.author: proposer

critic_notes.rationale: This is a linear rank-sum of two separately published anomalies (book-to-market and Boudoukh–Michaely–Richardson–Roberts net payout yield) with no genuine interaction — the "intersection" story is not what SUMRANK computes, since a firm extreme on one leg alone lands in the tails.

Adding net repurchases to earnings in the numerator of a market-cap-scaled yield is arithmetically just E/P plus net-payout-yield, i.e. a known-anomaly sum rather than a cross-theme interaction, and the un-COALESCEd prstkc/sstk will silently drop firms that report neither (economically zero-flow firms), biasing coverage inconsistently with the sibling proposals.

The conditional construction is thoughtfully sign-aligned, but (i) the hypothesis says off-diagonal cells carry "no signal" while the expression actually assigns cheap-issuers a negative and rich-repurchasers a positive score, and (ii) buyback drift concentrated in high book-to-market firms is a long-published result (Ikenberry–Lakonishok–Vermaelen; Peyer–Vermaelen), so this is close to a rediscovery; the /at inside both INDICATORs is also redundant since only the sign matters.

Economically the most coherent pairing here (enterprise multiple with total net external financing), but both components are published anomalies (Loughran–Wellman; Bradshaw–Richardson–Sloan) and SUMRANK imposes no interaction whatsoever, so the test cannot distinguish the joint mechanism from the additive average of two known effects, while dltis/dltr sparsity will erode coverage.

The persistence-of-financing-state dimension is a genuinely non-obvious refinement over one-shot issuance measures and the multiplicative form does concentrate the long leg in the cheap-and-committed corner, but the short leg degenerates into a large mass of exact zeros (all non-repurchasers plus all expensive firms), which risks unstable portfolio composition, and the 5-year TS_SUM plus un-COALESCEd prstkc/sstk will cut coverage materially.

The expression's natural direction contradicts the stated story: because the P/B rank multiplies a signed issuance average, the extreme long leg is populated by high-multiple *repurchasers* (large negative product), not by value firms, so the tested spread is glamour-buyback versus glamour-dilution rather than the intended valuation-conditioned dilution effect — and the underlying net-issuance anomaly is already well documented (Pontiff–Woodgate, Daniel–Titman).

Economically coherent and sign-consistent (the near-complementary indicators plus mirrored ranks reduce algebraically to ~1{net repurchaser} − RANK(ΔP/B), which still places contrarian repurchasers and post-run-up issuers in the correct diagonal corners), and conditioning on the *change* in the multiple rather than its level is a genuine departure from the gen-0 HML-clone designs — though the tester should verify the result is not simply annual return reversal interacted with the well-known net-issuance dummy.

The within-firm valuation-rank conditioning is a legitimately novel and well-motivated way to strip the permanent value tilt, but the expression collapses to approximately TS_RANK(B/M) − 1{net issuer}, so roughly half the cross-sectional variation is a plain net-share-issuance dummy (a published anomaly) and the 5-observation TS_RANK is very coarse; the claimed "conditional" interaction is really additive.

A clean, internally consistent pure interaction (sign driven by the buyback change, magnitude scaled by cheapness) that directly diagnoses why the archived level-based version had a flat slope, but it remains a one-input variant of that archived signal, and using market cap in both the valuation rank and the financing denominator risks a mechanical price-driven correlation.

Sign convention is correct (product is non-negative, high = expensive plus erratic issuance, expected negative) and financing second moments are unexplored here, but issuance volatility is strongly correlated with issuance level and with small young growth firms, so the test may largely rediscover the net-issuance/asset-growth anomaly interacted with size unless that overlap is controlled.

The two legs use different constructs (dividend yield long versus price-to-book short), so the spread is essentially a value/high-yield-versus-glamour portfolio gated on the change in the liability ratio — i.e., a combination of the published dividend-yield, book-to-market and net-external-financing/asset-growth anomalies — and the stated coverage motivation does not justify the incoherent long/short asymmetry.

Since RANK(P/B) ≈ 1 − RANK(B/M) and the two five-year counts nearly sum to five, the expression algebraically reduces to ~5·RANK(B/M) + (buyback years) − 5, so the claimed interaction cancels and the signal reintroduces a full-strength cross-sectional value main effect — precisely the HML exposure that produced the archived version's negative FF5 alpha — making this a mirrored restatement of SerialRepurchaser_Cheapness_Persistence rather than a substantive repair.

This is essentially the archive's FinancingInformativeness_ScaledByCheapness with the continuous cheapness weight replaced by a hard median gate, and the underlying variable is the well-published net-share-issuance/buyback anomaly; the claim that the spread is "value-neutral by construction" is also overstated, since within the cheap half repurchasers still tilt to higher BM than issuers.

Beyond being the complementary subsample of Signal 1 (same net-issuance anomaly, different gate), the stated motivation misreads the archive: Glamour_FinancingInstability's +2.7% alpha was in the *opposite* direction to its expected sign, i.e. glamour issuers outperformed, which contradicts the positive sign asserted here.

Internally consistent, high-coverage, and the coverage-vs-economics diagnostic is a legitimate motivation, but the core predictor is the known liability/asset-growth anomaly and it overlaps substantially with the archive's IndustryCheap_NetCapitalReturn_Gate, so it should be judged as a robustness test rather than a new mechanism.

The conditioning direction is genuinely reversed relative to everything in the archive, non-issuers are correctly parked at zero so the tails are cheap-vs-expensive issuers rather than issuers-vs-non-issuers, and expression, hypothesis and negative sign all line up — though negative-book-equity firms in the P/B ratio need care beyond 1% winsorization.

A size-subsample restriction of Signal 1 is a cosmetic variant of an already-marginal design, it re-tests the well-documented fact that the issuance anomaly is stronger in small caps, and halving the already thin ~0.13 coverage invites exactly the sparse-coverage instability the objective warns against.

MIN of two non-negative flows makes the signal weakly positive with a huge tied mass at zero, so the long leg is an arbitrarily ordered pile of non-payers/non-issuers rather than an economic portfolio, and because sstk is dominated by small option-exercise proceeds for many firms the MIN will frequently collapse to a plain dividend-yield-times-multiple measure rather than capturing the intended "financing incoherence" state.

This is a single-input swap on the archive's one winner, and the swap makes the shortfall term ≈ negative change in book equity (clean-surplus identity), so the "test" mostly rediscovers the equity-shrinkage/retained-earnings dimension rather than isolating the cash-coverage mechanism the reasoning claims.

A modest but legitimate identification exercise — the hard median gate cleanly separates the interaction from a valuation-weighted main effect and the sign logic is internally consistent — though it is close to a construction variant of the archived winner and mirrors gating patterns already tried in the archive.

The mechanical argument is actually sound (a debt-funded buyback leaves EV roughly unchanged while mechanically inflating P/B), so replacing the conditioning multiple with EV/sales is a substantive de-contamination rather than cosmetic, but it remains one axis of the same archived family and EV/sales carries strong persistent industry-level variation that will dominate the gate.

Smoothing the cash-generation benchmark to a three-year mean is directly implied by the "chronic external dependence" claim rather than decorative, and the expression matches the hypothesis and sign, but it is still an incremental refinement of the archived winner with a predictable modest effect on precision.

The hypothesis is about time-varying issuance windows, but level-minus-industry-demeaned recovers the industry *mean level* of sstk/at, which is dominated by persistent cross-industry composition (biotech vs utilities) and by option-exercise proceeds — so the expression measures industry identity, not a hot-market wave, and the interaction risks being a disguised industry-tilt bet.

The materiality threshold and sales-based multiple are targeted repairs of two real defects in the flat archived issuer-valuation signal, but the underlying claim that issuance underperformance concentrates in richly valued firms is close to the published Loughran-Ritter/Daniel-Titman result, so novelty is limited and the sstk-based gate still mixes SEOs with routine share sales.

Not a rediscovery and internally consistent (the gate correctly restricts both tails to material distributors), and while it is an incremental refinement of the archive's best signal rather than a new mechanism, it is a well-posed identification test of whether the archived alpha was merely a rich-firms-with-weak-operating-cash-flow effect.

The construction is coherent (rank multiplier is strictly positive so the sign is carried by payout×liability growth, with non-payers correctly near zero) and it substitutes an observed funding source for the oancf benchmark, though the Δ(lt/at) term is heavily contaminated by the known asset-growth/liability-growth anomaly and the triple product will be noisy.

This is a reweighting of the archived MaterialIssuers_RelativeSalesMultiple by issuance magnitude inside the same 2%-of-assets gate — a largely cosmetic variant whose incremental variation is the net-share-issuance anomaly itself, and whose flat-FMB diagnosis (no continuous variation) is not obviously cured since the archived signal already had continuous z-score variation.

Gating an industry-relative price-to-sales z-score on being a material repurchaser is essentially the value anomaly evaluated within the repurchaser subsample, which is a direct rediscovery of the long-documented result that buyback drift is concentrated in low-valuation ("value") repurchasers (Ikenberry-Lakonishok-Vermaelen; Peyer-Vermaelen), and the cross-theme content reduces to a sample filter.

Payout *composition* conditional on richness is a channel untouched in the archive and the negative sign is defensibly motivated by the archive's dividend-versus-total-payout reversal, but the expected sign runs against the well-documented positive repurchase-yield anomaly (so it is a genuine sign gamble) and interaction_type is mislabeled "ratio" for what is a product.

A five-year cumulative net equity issuance measure is the Daniel-Titman composite issuance anomaly, and since the RANK multiplier is strictly positive and monotone the signal will largely load on that known main effect rather than on any genuine valuation interaction.

Internally consistent and a genuine design change (continuous two-sided activity weight rather than a one-sided sample gate), but the sign is driven entirely by an industry-relative price-to-sales multiple — a known value anomaly — so the test hinges on whether the ABS(flow) weight adds anything beyond concentrating the tails in high-activity (and hence smaller, more volatile) firms.

This is the archive's MaterialIssuers_RelativeSalesMultiple with the sign relabelled and the gate symmetrized, and it is also largely redundant with Proposal 1's continuous version of the same interaction, so it adds little beyond a hard-versus-soft-gate cosmetic contrast.

A defensible metric-axis variation on Proposal 1 with an economically better-motivated valuation anchor (cash-flow yield rather than sales), though it inherits the same risk of being a repackaged industry-relative value signal and pays a real coverage penalty that will confound the metric-versus-sample interpretation the reasoning claims to resolve.

This is the archive's OpportunisticallyTimedIssuance_Stock with only the scaling denominator changed, and the expected sign has been reversed post hoc to match that signal's realized outcome, with an ad hoc "factor models mechanically short these firms" story replacing the prior hypothesis — that is sign-fitting, not a new test.

A legitimate mirror-image control with substantive refinements over the failed count-based predecessors (magnitude weighting, market-cap scaling, own-history MA benchmark), but the five-year accumulated repurchase level largely reproduces the published net-share-issuance/buyback anomaly, so the incremental content rests entirely on the own-valuation timing filter that has already come up empty twice in this archive.

The construction does match the stated hypothesis (good timers positive, bad timers negative, inactive near zero), but note that the SUB of TS_RANK(P/B) and TS_RANK(B/P) is algebraically just a centered monotone transform of a single term, so the "two-sided differencing" framing is cosmetic, and the long leg deliberately includes high-multiple issuers whom the documented issuance anomaly says should underperform.

Internally consistent and cleanly motivated as a coverage/subsample disentanglement of the archive's winning anchor, but it is only a numerator swap (oancf→ebitda) in an otherwise identical construction, so it is a robustness check rather than a new mechanism and should be judged as such.

This is a monotone re-scaling of the amplifier rather than a substantive change, and because RANK assigns the median firm a weight of ~0.5 instead of ~0 it flattens the interaction so much that the signal collapses toward plain industry-relative cash-flow yield — i.e. a rediscovery of the value anomaly with a mild tilt.

Testing whether the amplifier is a persistent policy state versus a one-year event is a legitimate economic question that the earlier count-based chronic-engagement attempt confounded with a weak sales anchor, though a three-year moving average of the same variable remains a modest, low-information-content refinement.

A well-designed discriminant test that shares no equity-flow information with the winner and would genuinely identify whether the channel is management trading its own shares, but |Δ(lt/at)| is also a generic balance-sheet-churn/volatility proxy, and the proposal is explicitly framed around an expected null, which serves diagnosis more than the objective of finding reliable alpha.

Gross issuance-plus-repurchase volume is economically distinct from absolute net flow precisely for simultaneous issuers/repurchasers, so this is a substantive and internally consistent test of "participation" versus "net supply change," with the caveat that gross flow scaled by assets tilts toward small, high-issuance firms and will need a size/volatility diagnostic.

It targets a real mechanical contamination — equity transactions move the market-cap denominator of the cheapness anchor — with an enterprise-level anchor that also restores full coverage, and it is constructed differently enough from the archive's conditional enterprise-flow signal not to be a rediscovery, though EV still contains market cap so the invariance claim is only partial.

This is a near-cosmetic recombination of two already-tested amplifier tweaks (gross vs. net, 1-year vs. 3-year MA) applied to the identical anchor, so it adds no new economic content and its expected gain over the two parents (t=3.48 and t=3.16) is within noise.

Summing two differently-scaled winsorized ratios with an arbitrary implicit 50/50 weight cannot attribute the effect to either channel (a dilution and a genuine equity-specific mechanism produce the same outcome), and both parents are already in the archive with t≈3.7, making this a recombination rather than a test of a distinct hypothesis.

Pairing the leverage-invariant enterprise anchor with the best-performing amplifier is a genuinely untested combination whose main purpose — separating the mechanism from the post-1988 oancf coverage subsample — is a real robustness question rather than a cosmetic variant.

Blending the strong oancf anchor with an anchor the archive already showed to be materially weaker (fmb 2.02) is as likely to dilute as to denoise, and the construction is internally awkward — a global SUMRANK is then industry z-scored, mixing two incompatible normalizations of an already-uniform variable.

A clean one-sided decomposition of the archive's best amplifier is the right attribution test at this stage, though it overlaps partially with the earlier failed FinancingInformativeness_ScaledByCheapness (cheapness × net repurchase/at, fmb 0.40) and with the known repurchase/payout-yield anomaly, so a positive result must be shown to be incremental to both.

The matched-construction mirror leg is the sharpest available test of whether the effect is symmetric participation or one-sided managerial confirmation, and the expected positive sign — cheap heavy issuers outperforming expensive heavy issuers — is a defensible, falsifiable claim that runs against the naive net-issuance anomaly reading and is therefore informative either way.

This is a mechanical splice of two archived variants whose leg decomposition already showed the repurchase and issuance amplifiers to be statistically indistinguishable (fmb 3.606 vs 3.613), so restricting the surprise to the issuance leg is a cosmetic recombination rather than a test of a new economic distinction — and the near-identical stats across every non-negative amplifier tried suggest the whole family is largely a magnitude-weighted rescaling of the same cash-flow-yield value signal.

The archive's two enterprise-anchored variants (gross turnover and net |activity|) already returned the identical fmb of 2.021 and near-identical alphas, strongly implying the enterprise anchor dominates and the amplifier's exact construction is immaterial, so swapping gross turnover for the issuance leg is a low-information variant rather than the coverage breakthrough claimed.

Earnings-to-price is a genuinely untested anchor in this pair's archive and the proposal is honest that it is a discriminating diagnostic (cash-specific mechanism vs. post-1988 sample), though prior evidence that both full-panel equity-based anchors (sales, EBITDA-to-price) were inert makes a null result the likely outcome and the informational value largely negative.

Putting market cap in the denominator of both terms makes the product load mechanically on 1/P², so any apparent improvement will be confounded with a low-price/microcap tilt and the signal ceases to be interpretable as valuation × participation — the exact contamination the proposal concedes but does not design around.

The state-vs-event contrast is a legitimate open question with the now-working cash anchor, and the bounded 0–5 count is the one amplifier that does not merely rescale the value score by transaction magnitude, though it overlaps conceptually with the already-tested within-industry activity indicator (fmb 3.27) and so is more of a robustness probe than a new mechanism.

The stated purpose — determining whether debt raising amplifies cheapness as strongly as equity raising — cannot be answered by an expression that adds sstk and dltis into a single amplifier dominated by the already-tested equity term; a debt-issuance-only amplifier would be the internally consistent test.

A legitimate, coherent cell of the anchor×amplifier grid that has genuinely not been run and targets the leading signal's real weakness (0.091 coverage), but it is a third amplifier variant on an anchor already tested twice (gross turnover t=2.63, activity indicator t=2.00), so expected incremental information is modest and the family is accumulating serious multiple-testing debt.

Internally consistent and worth one run, but the honest diagnosis of EarningsYield_x_GrossTurnover is that its +3.8% alpha with fmb t=0.057 signals an alpha driven by a few extreme weight observations rather than a monotone cross-sectional slope, and swapping a bounded 0–5 count for the continuous weight is as likely to reveal that the alpha was a weighting artifact as to confirm the mechanism — which is informative, but the proposal oversells it as "highest expected value."

The conditioning-versus-weighting distinction is a real and worthwhile test, but it is close kin to HighlyActiveFirms_CashYieldCheapness (already an indicator gate, fmb 3.27, alpha 3.4%), and the strict count>4 gate zeroes out most of the panel, creating a large tie mass at zero that can make decile breakpoints and the resulting long-short spread degenerate rather than "most stable" as claimed.

Because dvt/at alone clears the 0.02 threshold for the large majority of dividend payers, the counter collapses in practice to a dividend-payer/dividend-persistence indicator, so the test conflates the participation mechanism with the well-known dividend-payer characteristic (and its size/profitability/low-volatility loadings), and the stated defense that "no single component can dominate by scale" is wrong — the components are summed *inside* the indicator, so dividends can trigger it unilaterally.

A clean directional decomposition of the winning amplifier whose expected sign is consistent with the expression's natural direction and is not a repackaged buyback-yield effect, though the reviewer should note that sstk is heavily contaminated by routine option-exercise and ESPP flows, so a positive result may identify equity-comp-intensive firms rather than genuine serial issuers under market discipline.

This is the most substantively motivated proposal in the set — it isolates a specific mechanical contamination (repurchases shrink market cap and mechanically inflate the equity-based cash yield that is then multiplied by transaction persistence) rather than permuting grid cells — with the caveat that oancf is reported net of interest paid, so the hypothesis's claim that it "accrues to all capital providers" is not strictly correct and the EV denominator is only approximately matched.
